title: Kwete Maize Beer
author: Maama Nakato
desc: A hundred and fifty grams of maize flour worked into a dough with a hundred millilitres of water, roasted to golden brown, mixed into a litre of boiled water, boiled fifteen minutes, cooled to forty-five degrees and fermented a day.
longDesc: This is the Kampala kwete, made from maize with malted millet, and it carries the most precise quantities of any Ugandan drink in print — because a team of food scientists measured what fermentation does to the aflatoxins in Ugandan maize. The answer is remarkable: a thousand-fold reduction, and no detectable aflatoxin after twenty-four hours. The stated endpoint is a pH of four or below with a titratable acidity of at least zero point two per cent, and the taste is slightly alcoholic, thick and sweet-sour.
ingredients: 150 g hulled maize flour, for the dough
2% by volume prefermented maize porridge, as the starter
// The WHO records a traditional ratio of equal parts maize flour and germinated millet
equipment: Saucepan or flat pan, for roasting
steps: Mix the 150 g of hulled maize flour with the 100 ml of water to form a dough.
Roast the dough to golden brown in a saucepan over a hotplate. No temperature is documented — golden brown is the cue.
Mix the roasted dough into 1 litre of boiled water.
Inoculate with 2 per cent by volume of prefermented maize porridge.
It is ready at a pH of 4.0 or below with a titratable acidity of at least 0.2 per cent by weight. The measured result is a mean pH of 3.9 and an acidity of 0.6 per cent.
It should be slightly alcoholic, thick in consistency, with a sweet-sour taste.
chefTips: The stated endpoint — pH at or below 4.0 with a titratable acidity of at least 0.2 per cent — is the clearest documented process target of any Ugandan drink. Without a meter, the sweet-sour taste and the thick consistency are the same signal.
Golden brown is the roasting cue. No temperature exists for it in any source.
Cool to forty-five degrees before inoculating. Hotter and you kill the starter.
The starter is two per cent of prefermented maize porridge — a spoonful of a previous batch into a litre. That is back-slopping and it is what gets you a reliable twenty-four-hour ferment.

Aflatoxins are the real story here. Maize in Uganda has been reported at levels up to 19 mg/kg, and the authors' own earlier work found 22.2 micrograms per kilo in Kampala households. Fermentation produced an over thousand-fold reduction in aflatoxins B1, B2, G1 and G2, with none detectable after 24 hours, and Lactobacillus rhamnosus bound 83.5 per cent of aflatoxin B1. Lactic fermentation reduces aflatoxins rather than concentrating them, and that is worth knowing about every fermented grain food in this collection.
The WHO records the traditional ratio as equal parts maize flour and germinated millet, which is the household version of the same drink.
Kidongo is made from kwete residue, with water and brown sugar added and fermented overnight. The WHO notes plainly that it is not a popular drink.
This is not the Lugbara kwete, UGA087, which is sorghum raised with aku fi. Two drinks, one name, and they should not be merged.
commonMistakes: Inoculating while it is still hot.
Roasting the dough past golden to dark brown.
Fermenting it cold, so it never acidifies.
Assuming it is the same drink as the Lugbara kwete.
sources: Adapted from 'Probiotic Enrichment and Reduction of Aflatoxins in a Traditional African Maize-Based Fermented Food', MDPI Nutrients 2019, 11(2):265 — the 150 g of hulled maize flour to 100 ml of water, the roast-to-golden-brown step, the litre of boiled water, the 15-minute boil, the cooling to 45 degrees, the 2 per cent by volume prefermented-porridge inoculum, the 24-hour fermentation at 30 degrees, the stated endpoint of pH at or below 4.0 with titratable acidity of at least 0.2 per cent by weight, the achieved mean pH of 3.9 and 0.6 per cent acidity, and the slightly alcoholic, thick, sweet-sour description are all from that paper.

The aflatoxin findings are from the same paper: Ugandan maize reported up to 19 mg/kg, the authors' earlier finding of 22.2 plus or minus 4.6 micrograms per kilo in Kampala households, an over thousand-fold reduction of aflatoxins B1, B2, G1 and G2 with none detectable after 24 hours, and 83.5 per cent aflatoxin B1 binding efficiency for Lactobacillus rhamnosus.

The traditional processing survey is C. Muyanja and B. S. Namugumya, 'Traditional processing, microbiological, physiochemical and sensory characteristics of kwete, a Ugandan fermented maize based beverage', AJFAND, covering divisions of Kampala district — 24-hour sourdough fermentation, a roasting step, 24-to-72-hour final fermentation at ambient temperature in metallic drums, 80 per cent of households consuming within 24 to 48 hours, and a final pH of 3.35 after 72 hours.
The equal-parts maize flour and germinated millet ratio, and the kidongo by-product fermented overnight with water and brown sugar, are from the WHO Global Status Report on Alcohol 2004.
This is a different drink from the Lugbara sorghum kwete in UGA087. The two are deliberately not merged.
storage: Drunk within a day or two. Eighty per cent of households consume it within 24 to 48 hours.
healthBenefits: Lactic fermentation produced an over thousand-fold reduction in aflatoxins in the documented trial.
Fermentation raises the availability of the maize's minerals and adds live lactic acid bacteria.
Coliforms disappeared within 24 hours of fermentation in the survey data.
Used as a social drink, an energy source, a thirst quencher and a weaning food.
culturalNote: That the best-quantified Ugandan drink recipe exists because scientists were studying aflatoxin in school feeding programmes is a good reminder of where documentation actually comes from. Maize porridge is the staple breakfast across Ugandan primary and secondary schools, which is why the contamination question mattered enough to measure.
